title: Persistent Neck Mass in an Adult
description: Recognize a neck mass at increased risk of cancer, skip empirical antibiotics, image with contrast, examine the upper aerodigestive tract, and use FNA rather than open biopsy, never assuming a cystic mass is benign.
objectives: Identify features that put a neck mass at increased risk of malignancy
Avoid empirical antibiotics without signs of bacterial infection
Order contrast CT or MRI and examine the larynx, tongue base, and pharynx
Choose fine-needle aspiration over open biopsy
Keep investigating a cystic mass and examine under anesthesia before any open biopsy

references.citation: Pynnonen MA, Gillespie MB, Roman B, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Evaluation of the Neck Mass in Adults. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2017;157(2_suppl):S1-S30.

Tandon S, Shahab R, Benton JI, et al. Fine-needle aspiration cytology in a regional head and neck cancer center: comparison with a systematic review and meta-analysis. Head Neck. 2008;30(9):1246-1252.
Goldenberg D, Begum S, Westra WH, et al. Cystic lymph node metastasis in patients with head and neck cancer: An HPV-associated phenomenon. Head Neck. 2008;30(7):898-903.

start.text: A 52-year-old man has a painless lump in the left upper neck that he noticed 5 weeks ago. He has had no sore throat, fever, or dental problems. The mass is 3 cm, firm, and slightly fixed.

risk.text: How do you approach this mass?

options.label: A 2-week course of antibiotics, then review
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: do not routinely prescribe antibiotics for a neck mass unless there are signs and symptoms of bacterial infection. He has none. His mass has been present at least 2 weeks without an infectious history, and it is firm, fixed, and larger than 1.5 cm, all markers of increased cancer risk.

options.label: Treat it as a mass at increased risk of malignancy and explain why to him
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: a mass present for 2 weeks or more without significant fluctuation or an infectious cause, or with fixation, firm consistency, size over 1.5 cm, or skin ulceration, is at increased risk for malignancy. Explain the significance and the planned tests to the patient, and avoid empirical antibiotics without signs of bacterial infection.

options.label: CT (or MRI) of the neck with contrast
Examine the larynx, tongue base, and pharynx, or refer to someone who can
Open excision biopsy of the node as the first tissue test
Ultrasound follow-up in 3 months before any biopsy

workup.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: order neck CT or MRI with contrast for a mass at increased risk of malignancy (strong). Perform or refer for a targeted examination that visualizes the mucosa of the larynx, tongue base, and pharynx. Use fine-needle aspiration rather than open biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain. In a meta-analysis of 3,459 head and neck aspirates, FNA was 89.6% sensitive and 96.5% specific.

cystic.text: CT shows a cystic mass. FNA returns thin fluid with scant inflammatory cells and no malignant cells. The pharynx looked normal. Next?

options.label: Reassure him: a benign branchial cleft cyst
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: for a cystic mass at increased risk of malignancy, continue evaluation until a diagnosis is obtained, and do not assume it is benign. In Goldenberg 2008, 17 of 20 patients with cystic nodal metastases had tonsil or tongue-base primaries, and 87% of tested tumors carried HPV DNA.

options.label: Keep investigating: repeat or image-guided FNA and look for an oropharyngeal primary
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: continue evaluating a cystic neck mass until a diagnosis is obtained, and do not assume it is benign. Cystic nodal metastases are strongly associated with HPV-related tonsil cancer: 17 of 20 came from palatine or lingual tonsil primaries, and 87% of tested tumors carried HPV DNA (Goldenberg 2008).

nondiagnostic.text: Repeat FNA and imaging have not given a diagnosis, and no primary site is visible in clinic. What now?

options.label: Examination of the upper aerodigestive tract under anesthesia, before any open biopsy
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: when FNA, imaging, and ancillary tests have not given a diagnosis or found a primary site, recommend examination of the upper aerodigestive tract under anesthesia before open biopsy. Ancillary tests should be guided by history and examination.

options.label: Open excision of the neck mass
options.feedback: AAO-HNS 2017: examine the upper aerodigestive tract under anesthesia before open biopsy when FNA, imaging, and ancillary tests have not given a diagnosis or found a primary site.

eua.text: Repeat, ultrasound-guided FNA of the cyst wall shows squamous cell carcinoma, and examination under anesthesia finds a small primary in the left tonsil. He is referred to the head and neck cancer team.

fail_delay.text: Diagnostic Delay: Empirical antibiotics for a suspicious neck mass.

fail_biopsy.text: Guideline Deviation: Open biopsy before FNA and full evaluation.

fail_missed.text: Diagnostic Error: Cystic nodal metastasis dismissed as benign.

success.text: Case Complete: Suspicious neck mass worked up without delay.
